theme: I will extol you, my God and King
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 145. This is the last psalm of David in the Psalter, and the only one labeled “A Praise.” Read it as a response to the book of Esther, which never mentions God, by a psalm that does nothing else.
settingTheScene: Psalm 145 is an acrostic, with each verse beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, covering praise from A to Z. It sets the tone for the final five psalms, which are full of hallelujahs. After reading Esther, where God’s name is hidden, Psalm 145 shows that God’s character is plain: he is great, good, near, and faithful.
observation: “I will extol you, my God and King, and bless your name forever and ever” (v. 1).
“Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and his greatness is unsearchable” (v. 3).
“One generation shall commend your works to another, and shall declare your mighty acts” (v. 4).
“The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (v. 8).
“The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made” (v. 9).
“Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your dominion endures throughout all generations” (v. 13).
“The eyes of all look to you, and you give them their food in due season” (v. 15).
“The LORD is near to all who call on him, to all who call on him in truth” (v. 18).
interpretation:
The psalm is a sustained song of delight in God. David starts with a personal vow to praise every day, forever. But his praise is not private. “One generation shall commend your works to another.” The faith is passed along by telling.

The center of the psalm is verse 8, which echoes God’s self-revelation to Moses in Exodus 34:6: “gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.” This phrase recurs throughout the Old Testament as the summary of God’s character. You have met it in Nehemiah 9 and will find it in Joel and Jonah. David builds on it: God is good to all, and his mercy is over all he has made.

The psalm then celebrates his kingdom, which is everlasting. Human kingdoms rise and fall: Babylon, Persia, and so on. But God’s reign does not end. And yet this great King is near. He upholds all who are falling, raises those who are bowed down, and opens his hand to satisfy the desire of every living thing.

Verses 17 to 20 speak about God’s nearness and justice. “The LORD is near to all who call on him in truth. He fulfills the desire of those who fear him; he also hears their cry and saves them.” This is the answer for the diaspora. Even when God’s name is not on the page, he is near.

The psalm ends with the promise that the wicked will be destroyed, and the call for all flesh to bless his holy name forever. There is a stunning phrase in the Hebrew Bible: there is no verse starting with the letter “nun” in the standard Hebrew text, though some ancient copies have one. Even the most careful praise is not complete; there is always more to say.
connection: Exodus 34:6-7 is the source of the phrase in verse 8. Matthew 5:45 says that God makes his sun rise on the evil and the good. Matthew 6:33 promises that those who seek first the kingdom will be provided for. Luke 1:33 says of Jesus, “Of his kingdom there will be no end.” James 4:8: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.” Revelation 4:11 praises the Lord for creating all things.
application:
Read the psalm aloud as your morning praise. Let each verse draw you into worship.

Tell a younger person about something God has done for you. “One generation shall commend your works to another.”

Memorize verse 18, and pray it when you feel far from God.
prayerPrompts: Extol God as King, in your own words.
Tell him one thing he has done that you want to commend to another generation.
Thank him that he is near to all who call on him.
